synopsis: Mass and payload are central to off-road braking validation: grade and payload can change available deceleration by an amount comparable to the deceleration itself, while real machines face finite brake torque, thermal limits, load-induced balance changes and deformable ground—even though mass cancels in a friction-limited point-mass model [f145, f5900, f5887, f5888]. The recommended control policy limits commanded deceleration by stability, brake capacity and payload, with a jerk limit; validation must cover laden and unladen stopping, grade stability and behavior after stopping [f152, f11890]. Existing published MOSH closed-loop tests require unloaded machines on gradients of 1% or less, leaving loaded and slope cases uncovered, whereas Queensland stopping assumptions require fully laden vehicles and the worst relevant road, grade, tyre and brake-delay combination [f5564, f5565, f3403]. Physical validation should therefore test maximum payload and slopes, but the research identified no suitable facility or supplier for representative-speed testing of 50–400 t machines, and facility availability may independently constrain scheduling [f1610, f1166, f1167]. Transfer across machine families should use model-specific stopping curves by grade, load and surface, with validity records documenting mass and payload coverage; US FMVSS No. 127, limited to vehicles up to 4,536 kg GVWR, is an on-road reference rather than an applicable off-road requirement [f7017, f8005, f2831].
